jinan1_2022_jinan.label: Jinan-1 microsatellite to Jinan (Li et al. 2025), one constant calibrated
jinan1_2022_jinan.note: A 23 kg microsatellite with a 200 mm telescope and a 280 mm portable station. The paper does not state its atmosphere, pointing loss, background or transmit optics, so those are assumptions from other sources, and ONE constant - the station efficiency - is calibrated to the 25 September 2022 pass's peak count rate. What that pass then checks independently is the fall with elevation: 6.9 dB predicted against 6.6 measured to 13.9 degrees.
jinan1_2022_jinan.source: Li et al., 'Microsatellite-based real-time quantum key distribution', Nature 640, 47 (2025), arXiv:2408.10994. The pass figures used here (Fig. 4b, Table 1) are the preprint's, arXiv:2408.10994v1; the version of record reports up to 1.07 million bits in a single pass, where v1 said 0.59 million, and moves its per-pass results to Extended Data

finance_aml.notes: Reference architecture only, and no artifact of it is published. IBM's official Multi-PNA+EU was run here on this project's windows as a teacher (`scripts/train/ibm_multignn/`; test F1 0.6616 and 0.6878 in two runs of seed 1), and the compact GNN and the MLP are distilled from it. The page's graph model is `finance_aml.gnn_compact`, which reads a capped neighbourhood of 16 edges per transaction; message passing over the whole graph needs every account's neighbourhood at scoring time, which the browser does not hold. That is a choice for this operating point, not an impossibility: Bilgi et al. (arXiv:2610.18054v2, preprint) run an edge-centric GNN under CKKS on the IBM AML benchmark at 5.31 s per queried transaction (1.65 s amortized over a batch of 16) with HEonGPU on one RTX 5090, with the graph held in plaintext by the server - server-side evaluation only, since those figures exclude the client's encryption and decryption, key generation and network communication - and its encrypted and plaintext predictions agree on 99.25% of transactions. Kept as a spec for the architecture it names. It is not the best published figure on this split: the published version of MEGA (TMLR, see the ceiling) re-runs Multi-PNA at 67.35 +/- 2.89 on Small HI, below FraudGT, Multi-FraudGT and every MEGA variant in its table.

(J Clin Epidemiol 2016) ask for at least 200 of each before a flexible calibration curve, and Riley et al. (Stat Med 2021) show that such rules of thumb can still be too few. NO on the browser's evaluation sample, drawn from the same window with fewer than 200 events, which is why the page draws no curve there and says so. The CORP terms are reported regardless, because pool-adjacent-violators picks no bin count, so they are stable where a binned curve is not.

genomics.notes: WHAT RUNS UNDER CKKS: the full score, in both tiers. One person's effect-allele dosages at every variant are encrypted together in one CKKS ciphertext; the effect weights stay in plaintext and are applied by one multiply-plain; rotate-and-add sums the products into one slot, and the decrypted score is compared with a cut, the 90th percentile of the plaintext score over the bundled panel (the browser's 30 individuals, or the individuals the Python loader reads), by linear interpolation between order statistics. A demo cut, not a clinical threshold. Both tiers also score every panel individual encrypted and report the largest score deviation and how often the high-risk flag agrees with the plaintext one. Not a neural network, and presenting a genomic foundation model as a PRS method would be the most obvious credibility hole available. Evaluation must be stratified by genetic ancestry, and what is measured here is a distribution shift, NOT an AUROC drop: 1000 Genomes is a reference panel carrying no breast-cancer case/control status, so no AUROC is computable from it and genomics_prs.py records auroc=null rather than inventing one. PGS000072 is the breast-cancer score of Graff et al. (Nat Commun 12:970, 2021; CC BY 4.0): 187 genome-wide significant variants weighted by their log odds ratios. 183 of them have a 1000 Genomes phase 3 genotype for every one of the 2,504 individuals and are scored; the other 4 are left out, never filled in, and the dosage files and the payload name each with its reason. The finding is the by_super_population.*.frac_above_global_cut rows listed above: one globally-set high-risk cut flags a far larger share of one ancestry group than of another, a gap that allele-frequency and linkage-disequilibrium differences between the groups can produce on their own (Martin et al., Nat Genet 51:584, 2019), and which this panel, carrying no case/control status, cannot split into frequency and risk. Read those rows, not this sentence - they are recomputed on every training run, so no figure quoted in prose here can drift away from them. The published European AUROC comes from a phenotyped UK Biobank cohort, which is why it cannot be reproduced on this page.

achieved.baseline_gap_note: This scores far below the 0.901 ResNet-18 baseline. The reason is representational rather than cryptographic: 3,226 parameters over a 14x14 input is a REPRESENTATION choice, not a feasibility limit - and this note said 'a CKKS-feasibility budget' until Round 32, which overstated how forced it was. Kim et al. (arXiv:2506.15258) do HE chest-X-ray inference on a VQGAN latent at downsampling factor 8 rather than on pixels, so the alternative to downsampling 28->14 is re-representing the input. The browser already runs onnxruntime-web, so such an encoder would run locally in plaintext with no privacy loss. Recorded as the sixth falsifiable trigger in the additional-model decision in docs/deliverable-verification.md, not acted on - and note that f=8 on a 28x28 input gives 3.5x3.5, so the transfer is the open measurement rather than a citation. This sentence claimed the trigger existed for two rounds while the table held five rows and none of them was this one; the trigger was written, and the decision moved to a tracked file so the claim can be checked. Round 24 found it had been WORSE than that - a constant predictor, emitting one class for all 156 test images, with accuracy 0.730769 exactly equal to the majority-class rate and AUC 0.354, below random. It was invisible because the registry declared `auc` while the record stored `accuracy`, and because this student had neither protection its teacher already had: class-weighted loss and AUC-based model selection. In the browser each layer's output is decrypted, ReLU and average pooling run in plaintext in the client, and the class is the argmax of decrypted logits; the page's MPC argmax runs on the WDBC logistic regression, not on this CNN, and on logits the client has already decrypted. The full deployment's hybrid path, which runs a federated CNN of this shape rather than these weights, keeps ReLU on secret shares (MPyC) and pools each share locally; its masked conversion masks every CKKS slot the client can decode, and each run bounds the client's whole view (see qsh.mpc.secret_inference). In the browser each layer's bias is added under encryption and every slot but its outputs is masked and flooded before the client decrypts, so the client decrypts the layer outputs and nothing else. A separate path on the page runs one held-out image through this student with no activation in either party's hands: CKKS for the convolution and the dense layers, every slot masked before the client decrypts, and Polytune garbled circuits for the 800 ReLUs and the argmax; its class matched the clear network on all 156 test images. satellite_comms.notes: A LINEAR NEXT-STEP FORECASTER SINCE ROUND 86, trained by scripts/train/satellite_student_forecaster.py from the published teacher. The logistic student before it classified the teacher's flags from 8 rows and could not follow the retrained teacher, because a threshold on a forecast error is not linear in the window. A forecast is close to linear in the last rows, and Telemanom's thresholding needs nothing else. So the encrypted part is the forecast: six dot products with the last 8 z-scored rows, ridge-fitted to the teacher's own forecasts on its unlabelled training windows. The client decrypts the forecast and thresholds it with the teacher's procedure at the teacher's floor, in plaintext. The record holds the pipeline's event scores beside the teacher's over the whole test half, the forecast errors of both against persistence, and the same model fitted to the truth instead of the teacher. The page scores this student end to end on its published stretch: its forecasts in plaintext and under CKKS (encryptedLinearBatch), Telemanom's thresholding in a TypeScript port checked flag for flag against the Python, and ESA-ADB's scorer in a port checked against the Python. Its weights.json carries the z-score constants, because the thresholding works in raw units.

satellite_comms.notes: 19 columns is small enough to evaluate under CKKS as a single packed dot product, so the encrypted tier here runs on the published feature set rather than on a reduction of it - and it had room to spare. The student now fits over the QUADRATIC expansion of those features, 209 terms, still one packed dot product at unchanged multiplicative depth, because the expansion is a function of the plaintext input and is computed before encryption. The 209 terms pad to 256 slots, 16 times fewer than the ring's 4,096, so each ciphertext packs 16 rows and the slots set the batching (34 ciphertexts for 529 segments), not a limit on the feature map; the cipher was never the binding constraint here - the feature map was. Measured: minority-class F1 0.8649 -> 0.9043, AUC-PR 0.9275 -> 0.9681 (0.968055 against the teacher's 0.968107, equal at four decimals). The satellite page evaluates this student under CKKS in the browser on all 529 test segments, as a check of agreement with plaintext. metric.baseline_source: Architecture showcase, not a performance claim. On THIS project's synthetic telemetry neither quantum model beats the classical random forest (RF macro F1 0.987 vs variational QNN 0.467). Published results are MIXED, not uniformly below a random forest -- an earlier revision of this note claimed they were, and the very paper cited here contradicts it: Al-Kuwari et al. (arXiv:2509.14282) Table VIII reports a hybrid QLSTM at 94.7% accuracy / 94.7% F1 against their own random-forest baseline on the same generated data, at 81.5 to 82.6% accuracy by tree count (read at the source, 2026-11-12). This project's forest reaches macro F1 0.987 on its own generator; the metrics and the simulations differ, so the figures rank nothing, but this generator's classes separate more easily than theirs. What remains well-founded is caution about evaluation quality rather than a universal ranking: arXiv:2512.05069 was withdrawn by its own authors for evaluation that was 'insufficient to fully support the conclusions'. That single withdrawal is thin support for a field-wide claim, so the anchor is now a survey: Kaissar, Bou Nassif & Bouridane, Future Internet 18(5):234 (2026-04-27, CC BY 4.0, DOI 10.3390/fi18050234), systematic to January 2026, finds that 'most current approaches rely on simulated quantum environments and legacy datasets, while evaluation practices remain inconsistent across studies' - active but methodologically early, which is a different and better-founded statement than 'worse than a random forest'. The Al-Kuwari paper is now peer-reviewed: IET Quantum Communication 7(1), DOI 10.1049/qtc2.70028 (2026-02-23). And the nearest strong 2026 result is CLASSICAL, which corroborates the framing here - but it is a DIFFERENT problem and Round 46 stopped calling it the same one. IACR ePrint 2026/1282 reaches 96.9% recall / 97.6% precision with physics-aware temporal features plus XGBoost against 17.3% for static QBER thresholding - but its abstract, read at source, is entanglement-based BBM92, a 24-dimensional feature space over 30-second sliding windows, binary detection of blended sub-threshold attacks on simulated FSO telemetry. This model classifies 8 BB84 attack TYPES from per-session physical observables. Neither the protocol, the label space nor the feature space matches, so it is an anchor, not a baseline.

telecom_ids.notes: The published model and its headline accuracy are the random forest's. The quantum-kernel SVC and the variational QNN, recorded at training time and not run on the page, are BINARY attack-against-normal classifiers, each trained on its own smaller draw (60 and 120 rows per class), so their macro F1, 0.832 and 0.467, averages two classes; the QNN predicts attack for every row, and 0.467 is that constant predictor's score. On each one's own split and labels a forest trained the same way scores 1.0 and 0.990 (docs/measurements/telecom-quantum-like-for-like-2026-11-07.json). The SVC's kernel uses no entangling gate, so it is computable classically in closed form.

achieved.baseline_gap_note: There is no baseline number to have a gap to, and that is a deliberate registry decision rather than a missing measurement: the two figures usually quoted for this corpus (99.61% for a classical CNN, 99.71% for a hybrid quantum-classical Quan-ConvCNN, Wang/Fok/Thing) are ACCURACIES on the BINARY benign-versus-malicious task, and this model is judged on 9-class macro F1, so putting them in `baseline` would render an accuracy beside a macro F1 as though the two were the same scale. WHAT THE COMPARISON CAN AND CANNOT SAY. The 9-class anchors are the dataset paper's random forest at 99.48% accuracy on its top-10 features (Samarakoon et al., arXiv:2212.01298) and BiTAD (Future Internet 17(11) 482) at 0.9047. This model's 0.9979 is on 934,361 rows and its own stratified random split, and those figures are on the rows as published, so each is an anchor and not a head-to-head. WHAT THE ROWS SAY ABOUT THOSE FIGURES. On the 1,215,890 rows as published, inputs equal on the two copies of the flood cannot pass 0.7685, binary or nine-class, so a score above that rests on a column that differs between the copies. Those are `Unnamed: 0`, `Rank`, `Seq`, `Offset` and `IdleTime`. The dataset paper's top-10 inputs include `Seq` and `Offset`. Of Wang/Fok/Thing's 28 inputs exactly one, `Offset`, differs between the copies, and `published_inputs_check` fits this project's booster to them: on the binary task accuracy 0.9599 with `Offset` and 0.7643 without it. That measures what those columns can do on these rows and does not rerun those papers' models. Wang/Fok/Thing's fall across base stations, from above 98% to 78.23% and 74.28% for the classical CNN, has the same shape here: with the copies in place this booster scores 0.4199 and 0.6059, and with them out 0.9973 and 0.9877.

contradictory_copies.what_this_means: The published file holds the same 281,529 flows twice. The first base station's UDP-flood file also holds the traffic of the second base station's attacker towards the victim, labelled Benign; the second base station's file holds those flows labelled UDPFlood. The two copies agree on every column but the labels and the file-position columns, and in the two capture files the 421,471 packets behind them carry identical timestamps, which two separate capture points could not produce. In each attack file exactly one address pair carries the attack label, which is why the second attacker's flows came out Benign in the first file. On these rows no model reading flow statistics can pass 1 - 281,529 / 1,215,890 = 0.7685. The loader keeps the UDPFlood copy, which is what the traffic was, and removes the Benign one; `as_published` repeats the same fit without that removal.

file_label_counterfactual.what_this_means: `IdleTime` holds 17 values, all multiples of 128, the spacing of a 32-bit float at this size, one for each attack session and base station. Read as Unix times they fall between 13 and 15 September 2022, and the dataset paper gives the captures as 26 and 29 August 2022, so the column does not measure anything about the flow: it names the file the flow came from, and each file is one attack. On the rows as published it was worth about 22 accuracy points, because it is one of the few columns that differs between the two copies of the flood described under `contradictory_copies`. On the cleaned rows it adds what is measured here, and that gain is still a model recognising the file. The shipped model does not read it.

achieved.framing: Real 5G network traffic, 9 attack classes, 46 flow-statistic features. This is a NETWORK-LAYER model and a different task from the QKD-layer classifier on the same page - no shared labels, no shared features, so the two scores are not a comparison. TWO CORRECTIONS MADE IN ROUND 86 EXPLAIN THE NUMBERS. The published file holds one attacker's UDP flood twice, the same 281,529 flows labelled Benign in one base station's file and UDPFlood in the other's; the Benign copies are removed, leaving 934,361 flows. And the model no longer reads `IdleTime`, which names the attack-session file a flow came from. Accuracy is 0.9979 and macro F1 0.9972. On the rows as published the same fit scores accuracy 0.7616, and no model reading these columns could pass 0.7685 there (`contradictory_copies`). `file_label_counterfactual` and `leak_counterfactual_accuracy` restore bookkeeping columns and reach about 1.0000, which is not a better model but a leak. `cross_base_station` trains on one base station and tests on the other: accuracy 0.9973 and 0.9877, against 0.4199 and 0.6059 on the rows as published. Two weak spots remain. Trained on the second base station, SYNFlood on the first scores F1 0.22. And without the TTL and hop columns, UDPScan across base stations falls to F1 0.05 (`without_ttl_and_hops`).

linear_baseline.what_it_is: multinomial logistic regression on the 36 NUMERIC features only, standardised, fitted directly rather than distilled. The 10 ordinal codes are excluded because their integer order is nominal and a linear model would read it as a magnitude. Recorded as the classical floor and as a feasibility probe for a future CKKS-linear tier: it predicts 9 of 9 classes, so a linear student on this corpus does not collapse the way an 8-class one nearly does elsewhere in this project.

achieved.metric_note: macro F1 and aggregate accuracy agree here, 0.9972 and 0.9979, and neither is the flattering one. They were far apart until the contradictory copies came out, 0.9275 against 0.7616, because the contradiction fell on the two largest classes. macro F1 stays the headline because the largest class is about 400 times the smallest. Read `per_class_f1` for what the two averages hide: SlowrateDoS is lowest at 0.9873, HTTPFlood is at 0.9934, and ICMPFlood, at 289 test rows, is at 0.9983. A linear model on the numeric columns reaches accuracy 0.9838 and macro F1 0.9691, so most of this is separable by a plane, which is what a corpus where each class came from its own tool against its own service should look like. The random split is the easier test: see `cross_base_station`.

No subsampling and no class rebalancing: `ICMPFlood` is 1,155 rows in the corpus and 289 in the test split, which is small but is the real prevalence, and resampling it would report a per-class F1 for a distribution the deployed model never sees. single_feature_leak_check.what_this_means: One-vs-rest rank-AUC per feature per class, at the 0.90 threshold scripts/prep_model_inputs.py already publishes against, measured AFTER all 67 drops. A LARGE NUMBER HERE IS EXPECTED ON THIS CORPUS AND IS NOT THE LEAK THIS MODEL IS ABOUT. The attacks are generated by distinct tools against distinct services, so a scan, a SYN flood and a slow-rate HTTP attack genuinely differ in TTL, packet rate, TCP window and ACK timing - these are the flow statistics an intrusion detector is supposed to use. The check's own docstring anticipates the case and warns rather than failing. The distinction that matters is against `leak_counterfactual_*`: `Unnamed: 0`, `Rank`, `Seq` and `Offset` cleared the same threshold while being bookkeeping columns that carry no information about the traffic at all, which is why those four are dropped and these are kept. The check cannot tell a file label from a statistic: `IdleTime` is out because its values name the attack session's file, which only reading the values showed, and `file_label_counterfactual` records what it was worth. Recorded rather than described so the distinction is checkable.

metric.baseline_source: Two published figures on 5G-NIDD are usually quoted - Wang, Fok & Thing report 99.61% accuracy for a classical CNN and 99.71% for a hybrid quantum-classical Quan-ConvCNN - and BOTH are accuracies on the BINARY benign-versus-malicious task, while this model is scored on 9 classes, which is why no number appears in `baseline`. The 9-class anchors are the dataset paper's random forest at 99.48% accuracy on its top-10 features (Samarakoon et al., arXiv:2212.01298) and BiTAD (Future Internet 17(11):482) at 90.47%. Caveats. (1) The Wang, Fok & Thing authors' own claim is about generalisation to UNSEEN attacks rather than about the headline; `references/REFERENCES.md` WS2 records this. (2) THOSE FIGURES ARE ON THE ROWS AS PUBLISHED, WHERE ONE ATTACKER'S FLOOD IS PRESENT TWICE UNDER CONTRADICTORY LABELS, and this model's are on the 934,361 rows left when the Benign copy is removed. (3) MEASURED HERE, on the rows as published, with an identical gradient-boosted model: accuracy 0.7616 with every identifier, every host fingerprint and the file label dropped, and no model reading those columns can pass 0.7685; 0.9829 with the file-label column `IdleTime` restored. On the cleaned rows it reaches 0.9979 without them. (4) A score above 0.7685 on the rows as published rests on a column that differs between the two copies, and those are the file-position columns: the dataset paper's top-10 inputs include `Seq` and `Offset`, and of Wang, Fok & Thing's 28 inputs exactly one, `Offset`, differs. Fitted to those 28, this project's booster scores binary accuracy 0.9599 with `Offset` and 0.7643 without it; that is not a rerun of their network. (5) When Wang, Fok & Thing train on one base station and test on the other, their accuracies fall from above 98% to 78.2-78.9% trained on base station 1 and 57.2-81.6% trained on base station 2 (their Tables V and VI), where the classical CNN, at 74.28%, beats four of the five hybrids. With the copies in place this project's booster falls the same way, to 0.4199 and 0.6059, and with them out it scores 0.9973 and 0.9877. These figures are an anchor and not a target that has been beaten or missed.

telecom_ids.notes: NETWORK-LAYER flow classification on real 5G traffic. This is a DIFFERENT TASK from the QKD-layer attack classifier on this same page, with zero overlap in label space or feature space, so neither score is the other's baseline. REFITTED IN ROUND 86 ON CLEANED ROWS AND WITHOUT THE FILE LABEL, the two facts that explain every number here. The published file holds one attacker's UDP flood twice, the same 281,529 flows labelled Benign in one base station's file and UDPFlood in the other's, and the Benign copies are removed. From Round 50 the model also read `IdleTime`, which names the file a flow came from, not anything the flow did. ACCURACY IS 0.9979 AND MACRO F1 0.9972 on 934,361 flows. On the rows as published the same fit scores accuracy 0.7616, no model reading these 46 columns can pass 0.7685 there, and training on one base station and testing on the other gives 0.42 and 0.61. On the cleaned rows that test gives 0.9973 and 0.9877 (`cross_base_station`). A LINEAR MODEL ON THE NUMERIC COLUMNS REACHES ACCURACY 0.9838, because each attack class was produced by its own tool against its own service. Two weak spots remain: trained on the second base station, SYNFlood on the first scores F1 0.22, and without the TTL and hop columns UDPScan across base stations falls to F1 0.05, since nmap's raw probes carry a TTL of their own. THE LEAK COUNTERFACTUALS ARE RECORDED EVERY RUN. Restoring the corpus's integer row identifiers or the file label takes accuracy to about 1.0000, a shortcut of the kind Engelen et al. (WTMC 2021) found in CIC-IDS2017. See M_NIDD's baseline_source for what that means for the published figures on these rows. NO STUDENT IS DISTILLED FROM THIS MODEL: the page's encrypted tier runs telecom_ids.student, distilled from the QKD-attack random forest (telecom_ids.qml).

metric.baseline_source: Architecture showcase, not a performance claim. On THIS project's synthetic telemetry neither quantum model beats the classical random forest (RF macro F1 0.987 vs variational QNN 0.467). Published results are MIXED, not uniformly below a random forest -- an earlier revision of this note claimed they were, and the very paper cited here contradicts it: Al-Kuwari et al. (arXiv:2509.14282) Table VIII reports a hybrid QLSTM at 94.7% accuracy / 94.7% F1 against their own random-forest baseline on the same generated data, at 81.5 to 82.6% accuracy by tree count (read at the source, 2026-11-12). This project's forest reaches macro F1 0.987 on its own generator; the metrics and the simulations differ, so the figures rank nothing, but this generator's classes separate more easily than theirs. What remains well-founded is caution about evaluation quality rather than a universal ranking: arXiv:2512.05069 was withdrawn by its own authors for evaluation that was 'insufficient to fully support the conclusions'. That single withdrawal is thin support for a field-wide claim, so the anchor is now a survey: Kaissar, Bou Nassif & Bouridane, Future Internet 18(5):234 (2026-04-27, CC BY 4.0, DOI 10.3390/fi18050234), systematic to January 2026, finds that 'most current approaches rely on simulated quantum environments and legacy datasets, while evaluation practices remain inconsistent across studies' - active but methodologically early, which is a different and better-founded statement than 'worse than a random forest'. The Al-Kuwari paper is now peer-reviewed: IET Quantum Communication 7(1), DOI 10.1049/qtc2.70028 (2026-02-23). And the nearest strong 2026 result is CLASSICAL, which corroborates the framing here - but it is a DIFFERENT problem and Round 46 stopped calling it the same one. IACR ePrint 2026/1282 reaches 96.9% recall / 97.6% precision with physics-aware temporal features plus XGBoost against 17.3% for static QBER thresholding - but its abstract, read at source, is entanglement-based BBM92, a 24-dimensional feature space over 30-second sliding windows, binary detection of blended sub-threshold attacks on simulated FSO telemetry. This model classifies 8 BB84 attack TYPES from per-session physical observables. Neither the protocol, the label space nor the feature space matches, so it is an anchor, not a baseline.
